topic: Attitude, Aptitude & Foundational Values, and Emotional Intelligence

items.title: Attitude — content, structure and functions
items.body:
An **attitude** is a learned, relatively enduring **evaluative orientation** (favourable/unfavourable) towards a person, object, idea or situation. Its **content** is what it is about; its **structure** is the classic **ABC model**:

| Component | Meaning | Governance example |
|---|---|---|
| **A**ffective | Feelings/emotions | Discomfort with corruption |
| **B**ehavioural (conative) | Action tendency | Reporting wrongdoing |
| **C**ognitive | Beliefs/thoughts | 'Transparency improves trust' |

Attitudes differ from **values** (abstract ideals, e.g., justice), **beliefs** (factual convictions) and **opinions** (verbal expressions). **Katz's functional theory (1960)** explains *why* we hold attitudes — they serve four functions:
- **Adjustment (utilitarian):** maximise rewards, minimise punishment.
- **Ego-defensive:** protect self-esteem from anxiety/conflict.
- **Value-expressive:** assert one's central values and identity.
- **Knowledge:** give structure and meaning to a complex world.

Attitudes vary in **valence** (positive/negative), **strength/centrality** and **complexity**; strong, central attitudes are hard to change and strongly guide behaviour.
keyPoints: Attitude = learned, enduring evaluative orientation towards an object, person or idea.
ABC structure: Affective (feelings), Behavioural/conative (action tendency), Cognitive (beliefs).
Distinguish attitude from values (abstract ideals), beliefs (facts) and opinions (verbal).
Katz's four functions: adjustment, ego-defensive, value-expressive, knowledge.
Attitudes vary in valence, strength/centrality and complexity; strong central attitudes resist change.
items.source: NCERT Psychology (Attitudes and Social Cognition); Katz (1960); Britannica — attitude

items.title: Attitude formation, change and the link with thought and behaviour
items.body:
**Formation:** attitudes are *learned*, not innate — through **classical and operant conditioning**, **observational learning/modelling**, **exposure** and **group/cultural transmission** (family, school, peers, media).

**Relation with thought and behaviour:** attitudes shape perception, memory and interpretation (cognition) and dispose us to act. But the **attitude–behaviour link is imperfect** — **LaPiere (1934)** showed hoteliers who served a Chinese couple later claimed they would refuse them. Attitudes predict behaviour best when they are **specific, strong, accessible** and free of strong situational pressure. Crucially, **behaviour also changes attitudes** (self-perception; dissonance reduction).

**Change mechanisms:**
- **Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957):** discomfort from inconsistent cognitions drives attitude change.
- **Persuasion:** communicated messages (see ELM note).
- **Direct/repeated experience** and **incentives**.

**Governance relevance:** a professed pro-citizen attitude must translate into responsive behaviour; training and role-modelling can reshape officials' attitudes towards transparency, gender sensitivity and service.
keyPoints: Attitudes are learned via conditioning, observation, exposure and group transmission.
LaPiere (1934) demonstrated the attitude–behaviour gap (stated intent ≠ actual action).
Attitudes predict behaviour best when specific, strong, accessible and free of situational pressure.
Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957) drives attitude change to restore consistency.
Behaviour can reshape attitudes; training/role-modelling can reorient officials' attitudes.

items.title: Moral and political attitudes
items.body:
A **moral attitude** evaluates persons, acts or policies against standards of **right and wrong**; it tends to be **strong, resistant to change** and anchored in core values (honesty, justice, non-violence). For a public servant it underpins **integrity** and the will to resist wrongdoing.

A **political attitude** is an evaluative orientation towards **political objects** — the state, the constitution, parties, ideologies, leaders and policies. It ranges along dimensions such as **liberal–conservative**, **left–right** and **authoritarian–democratic**.

**Sources — political socialisation:** family, school, peer groups, media, religion and significant events transmit political attitudes over a lifetime.

**Public-service caution:** a civil servant may privately hold political attitudes but must maintain **non-partisanship and neutrality** in duty. Moral and political attitudes can conflict — e.g., loyally implementing a lawful policy one personally dislikes — resolved by the ethic of serving the constitution and the public interest above private preference.
keyPoints: Moral attitude = evaluation against right/wrong; strong, value-anchored, resistant to change.
Political attitude = orientation towards state, parties, ideologies (liberal–conservative, left–right).
Political socialisation (family, school, peers, media) is the main source of political attitudes.
Civil servants may hold political attitudes privately but must stay non-partisan on duty.
Sound moral attitude underpins integrity and resistance to wrongdoing.
items.source: NCERT Political Science (political socialisation); NCERT Psychology

items.title: Social influence and persuasion
items.body:
**Social influence** is the process by which others change our thoughts, feelings or behaviour. Key forms:
- **Conformity** — yielding to group norms (**Asch's** line experiments); driven by *normative* (approval) and *informational* (accuracy) influence.
- **Compliance** — agreeing to a request; techniques include **foot-in-the-door** and **door-in-the-face**.
- **Obedience** — following authority (**Milgram's** experiments), which warns against unethical 'just-following-orders' conduct.
- **Kelman's processes:** compliance → identification → **internalisation** (genuine acceptance).

**Persuasion — Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986):**

| Route | Basis | Durability |
|---|---|---|
| **Central** | Effortful scrutiny of argument quality | Lasting, predicts behaviour |
| **Peripheral** | Surface cues (credibility, attractiveness, repetition) | Transient |

Persuasion depends on **source** (credibility, likeability), **message** (quality, two-sided, fear appeals used carefully) and **audience** (motivation, ability). **Governance use:** behaviour-change communication (immunisation, sanitation, tax compliance) works best via credible messengers and the central route; officials must also recognise manipulation and resist it.
keyPoints: Social influence forms: conformity (Asch), compliance (foot-in-the-door), obedience (Milgram).
Normative vs informational influence explains why people conform.
Kelman's three processes: compliance, identification, internalisation.
ELM (Petty & Cacioppo): central route = argument scrutiny (durable); peripheral = surface cues (transient).
Persuasion factors: source credibility, message quality, audience motivation/ability.
Behaviour-change governance campaigns work best through credible messengers and the central route.
items.source: Asch (1951); Milgram (1963); Kelman (1958); Petty & Cacioppo (1986); NCERT Psychology

items.title: Aptitude and foundational values for civil service
items.body:
**Aptitude** is the natural or acquired **capacity** to learn and perform a role; **civil-service aptitude** combines analytical ability with the temperament and values that public office demands. **Foundational values** are the ethical bedrock expected of every public servant (Second ARC; UPSC ethics framework):

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Integrity** | Wholeness — consistency between values and action; incorruptibility |
| **Impartiality** | Fairness among persons/interests, without favour |
| **Non-partisanship** | Political neutrality; serving the government of the day without party bias |
| **Objectivity** | Decisions on evidence and merit, not personal bias |
| **Dedication to public service** | Commitment to citizens' welfare above self-interest |
| **Empathy** | Understanding citizens' feelings and situations |
| **Tolerance** | Respect for diversity of views, faiths and identities |
| **Compassion** | Care for the suffering, especially the **weaker sections** |

The **Nolan Committee (UK)** codifies allied **Seven Principles of Public Life**: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership. These values convert legal authority into **legitimate, humane and trusted governance**.
keyPoints: Aptitude = capacity to learn/perform; civil-service aptitude blends ability with ethical temperament.
Integrity = consistency of values and action; impartiality = fairness among persons without favour.
Non-partisanship = political neutrality; objectivity = evidence/merit-based decisions.
Dedication to public service = citizens' welfare above self-interest.
Empathy, tolerance and compassion (esp. towards weaker sections) humanise administration.
Nolan Committee's Seven Principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
items.source: Second ARC, 4th & 10th Reports; Nolan Committee (UK) Seven Principles of Public Life

items.title: Emotional intelligence in administration and governance
items.body:
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the ability to **perceive, understand, manage and use emotions** — one's own and others'. The term was coined by **Salovey and Mayer (1990)** and popularised by **Daniel Goleman (1995)**, whose model has **five components**:

1. **Self-awareness** — recognising one's emotions and their impact.
2. **Self-regulation** — managing impulses and moods; staying calm under pressure.
3. **Motivation** — inner drive to achieve beyond money/status.
4. **Empathy** — sensing and considering others' feelings.
5. **Social skills** — building rapport, managing relationships and teams.

**Utilities in governance:**
- **Crisis and stress management** (disasters, law-and-order) with composure.
- **Conflict resolution** and negotiation with stakeholders.
- **Empathetic, citizen-centric service delivery**, especially for vulnerable groups.
- **Team leadership and motivation** of subordinates.
- **Ethical resilience** — resisting emotional manipulation, anger and the temptations behind corruption.

EI **complements** (does not replace) domain knowledge and legal competence; together they produce administrators who are both effective and humane. It is distinct from **IQ**.
keyPoints: EI = perceive, understand, manage and use emotions (self and others).
Term coined by Salovey & Mayer (1990); popularised by Goleman (1995).
Goleman's five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
Governance utilities: crisis/stress management, conflict resolution, empathetic delivery, team leadership, ethical resilience.
EI complements (not replaces) domain knowledge and legal competence; distinct from IQ.
items.source: Salovey & Mayer (1990); Daniel Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); Second ARC, 10th Report
